title: Replying to @Becca Silbar  #theatre #musicaltheatre #broadway #westend
transcript: What do I think of jukebox musicals where the story is also established IP, not just the songs? So taking pre-existing songs and putting them in a pre-existing story? As a general rule, I tend to think that this is the most treacherous kind of jukebox musical. And I say “treacherous,” not “worst,” for a couple reasons. One is that there are multiple ways of going around it. Something like Titanique, for example, even though I had some issues with the Broadway transfer, is more or less able to get away with stuffing these Celine Dion songs into the plot of Titanic because that is the joke of the show. I never thought I'd talk about & Juliet in the same sentence as Lazarus, one of the most bleak and heady jukebox musicals in existence. But one thing they have in common. (Probably THE one thing they have in common) is that they are both sequels to existing stories. So even though it's preexisting IP, they're not restricted by the plot structure. Because when you are sticking pretty closely to an established plot, you're basically doubling the challenge for yourself. Trying to make pre-existing songs work in a new narrative context is already the hurdle that every jukebox musical kind of faces. So when you don't even have flexibility on the narrative side, it's that much easier to end up feeling like the songs don't belong at all. And one of the worst examples of this, I think I've ever seen was the Bullet Over Broadway musical. Another one was the Roman Holiday musical, which I saw in San Francisco, one of its many attempts at a pre-Broadway engagement. I actually thought the show was beautiful to look at, and I even really liked the chemistry between the two leads. But every time they stopped to sing a Cole Porter song, the show felt like it was grinding to a screeching halt. The original jukebox musical version of Clueless that I talked about in that last video was also a pretty catastrophic example of this, even though they changed some of the lyrics like I talked about. Moulin Rouge kind of fits into this category too, even though the film it's based on was also a Jukebox musical. They swapped out so many of the songs for other ones that they ended up in this situation anyway. Kind of an unforced error,if you will, but I actually don't think that's the main problem with Moulin Rouge as an adaptation. But there are some musicals that face this problem head on and still manage to overcome it. Like I haven't seen Priscilla, Queen of the desert in 15 years, but I seem to recall that the songs felt pretty well integrated. Or at least they were fun and rousing enough to get away with pausing the story for a bit. Also have to mention that despite everything I just said, I would still probably rather see one of these jukebox adaptations, then another painfully formulaic biographical jukebox musical. Cause at least it's a bit of a new experiment every time. Like I know it sounds on the surface like “movie adaptation + Jukebox Musical” is like double laziness. But at least matching up a movie with an unrelated song book requires some imagination.
classificationReason: Title begins 'Replying to @Becca Silbar' — primary purpose is responding to a viewer comment with a general essay on jukebox musicals. No specific production is reviewed; Titanique, & Juliet, and Lazarus are cited only as examples in a broader argument.
